name: North Wahgi
confidence_why: The only first-hand description of North Wahgi (McLean & McLean 2005) calls stress unpredictable and marks it on initial, medial and final syllables, and Phillips 1976 analyses Wahgi stress as phonemic for the same reason, so the WALS coding of fixed final stress (Goedemans & van der Hulst) is a second-hand database entry contradicted by the very primary it cites. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Mc Lean 2005.
catalog_citation: Mc Lean, Heather and Don Mc Lean (facilitators). 2005. 'North Wahgi (Yu We) language [Western Highlands Province].' In Steve Parker (ed.), Phonological descriptions of Papua New Guinea languages (Data Papers on Papua New Guinea Languages 47), 33-38. Ukarumpa:…
catalog_quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is not written in the orthography. It is unpredictable but disyllabic names generally have the stress on the first syllable. Kere ‘girl’s name’ kere ‘little’ Kanjip ‘star, girl’s name’ kanjip ‘they saw’ Kupull ‘man’s name’ kupull ‘sky’ Kuru ‘girl’s name’ kuru ‘white’ Tone is not written as the meaning can usually be determined by the context: high [ ] low [ ] tone: ka ‘bird’ ka ‘good’ kamb ‘possum, small animal’ kamb ‘banana’ kanjip ‘star’ kanjip ‘they saw’ mi ‘north’ mi ‘taro’ mek ‘vomit’ mek ‘black bird of Paradise’

tone_statements.citation: Hamp, Eric P. 1958. Wahgi (New Guinea) prosodic phonemes. Oceania 29(1): 62-64.
tone_statements.quote: (2) Tome. There seem to be two tones that may occur with vowels—high and low. ... this phonetic high is best analysed as part of the allophones of an extra stress ; phonetic low is then added to the allophones of the other stresses. In this fashion the category of tone as such disappears from our roster of phonemes. ... Because the incidence of heavy stress is not completely predictable in terms of juncture (13-14), we distinguish a strong low-pitched stress /"/, which occurs with one syllable (rarely more) of most words. There is also a less frequent ... strong high-pitched stress /*/.

tone_statements.summary: Reanalyses Luzbetak's high vs low tone as two contrasting heavy stresses, high-pitched /*/ vs low-pitched /"/ (plus weak /'/), one per word as a rule; denies tone as a separate phonemic category.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is in the publisher PDF we hold exactly where the locator says (p.4 = printed p.36, 'Suprasegmentals'), verbatim apart from dropped IPA93 private-use stress/tone glyphs. (2) Deciding source: a 2005 SIL Organised Phonology Data sketch (6 pp) by the resident SIL team — first-hand and the most recent description of North Wahgi, but minimal. Its explicit words are 'unpredictable', so lexical is a faithful coding; Phillips 1976:31 (held for sister record nucl1620) independently analyses Wahgi stress as phonemic 'on the basis of its unpredictableness', which supports it. (3) The residual risk is real but unproven: every common-word member of the OPD's four stress pairs is final-stressed and every name initial-stressed, and WALS/StressTyp code the 'Wahgi (Banz)' lect — Banz being a North Wahgi village by the OPD's own list and Glottolog's dial
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again.— agree, confirmed in copies we hold. (McLean & McLean 2005, Data Papers PNG 47:33-38), p.4 = printed p.36, heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)': 'Stress is not written in the orthography. It is unpredictable but disyllabic names generally have the stress on the first syllable.' followed by the four name/common-word pairs and the tone pairs — verbatim (extracted text). Raw codepoints confirm the dropped glyph is IPA93 PUA U+F0C8 (= 0xC8, primary stress): ˈKere/keˈre, ˈKanjip/kanˈjip, ˈKupull/kuˈpull, ˈKuru/kuˈru, exactly as the compilers decoded. downloaded sources R

sources.citation: WALS Online, lect 'Wahgi' (wals_code wah; alt. name Banz; ISO whg;wgi): datapoints 14A Fixed Stress Locations = Ultimate, 15A = Fixed stress (no weight-sensitivity), 17A = Iambic (Goedemans & van der Hulst), refs Luzbetak 1956, Phillips 1976; 13A Tone = Simple tone system (Maddieson).
sources.quote: Second-hand database coding of a lect that straddles whg/wgi and names Banz (a North Wahgi village): fixed final (ultimate) stress. Its cited primary Phillips 1976:31 actually calls Wahgi stress phonemic/unpredictable; the other cited primary, Luzbetak 1956 (Banz dialect), is not held.
